procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated the 25th September, 1973 of the Allahabad High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 1809 of 1969.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Sessions Judge found the accused guilty under Section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced them to life imprisonment. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of the present appellants and acquitted Sileti Singh, the father. There was no appeal by the State against the acquittal.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants, whose conviction and sentence were confirmed by the High Court, appealed to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal.

directions: The appellants will forthwith surrender to their bail bonds
The appellants will be taken into the custody to serve out their sentence.

issue.issue_text: Whether the reasons stated by the High Court in acquitting Sileti Singh by giving the benefit of doubt are sound and convincing.

facts: The High Court acquitted Sileti Singh, giving him the benefit of the doubt.
The High Court's reasoning was that Sileti Singh's presence at the time of the commission of the offense was not established beyond a reasonable doubt.
The State did not file an appeal against Sileti Singh's acquittal.
law: An acquittal cannot be overturned by the Supreme Court if the State has not filed an appeal against it.
application: While hearing the appeal of the other two convicted accused, the Supreme Court reviewed the High Court's decision regarding Sileti Singh.
The Supreme Court explicitly disagreed with the High Court's reasoning for the acquittal.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court found that the reasons stated by the High Court for acquitting Sileti Singh were "not sound and convincing." However, because the State had not appealed the acquittal, the Supreme Court could not overturn the decision, and his acquittal had to stand.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the reasons stated by the High Court in acquitting Sileti Singh by giving the benefit of doubt are sound and convincing.
appellant_arguments: Not mentioned in the text. The appellants in this case were appealing their own convictions, not the acquittal of their co-accused, Sileti Singh.
respondent_arguments: Not mentioned in the text. The State (respondent) did not file an appeal against the acquittal of Sileti Singh.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A conviction based purely on circumstantial evidence is valid when the circumstances are so telling that the only reasonably possible conclusion is the guilt of the accused.
obiter: When dastardly crimes are detected and the offence is brought home to the accused, courts must deal with the offender ruthlessly and impose deterrent punishment.

The reasons stated by the High Court in acquitting another party, by giving him the benefit of doubt, were not sound and convincing, but since the State has not preferred an appeal, his acquittal will stand.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court found no merit in the appeal, holding that the conviction and sentence of the appellants were perfectly correct and sound. Based on a scrutiny of the evidence, the Court was in complete agreement with the findings of the Sessions Judge and the High Court that the case, though based on circumstantial evidence, led to the only reasonably possible conclusion: the deceased did not commit suicide but was brutally assaulted and then hung by the neck by the appellants to create the appearance of a suicide.
legal_tests_applied: The standard for conviction based on circumstantial evidence, which requires that the circumstances are so telling that the only conclusion reasonably possible is the one of guilt.
why_appellant_lost: The Supreme Court found itself in 'complete agreement with the findings entered by the Sessions Judge and the High Court regarding the cause of the death of the deceased and the manner in which she was done to death.'

The Court concluded that the circumstantial evidence was 'so telling that the only conclusion reasonabiy possible is the one arrived at by the courts below that the deceased did not commit suicide by hanging herself but was done to death by l)ein¥ brutually assaulted an~ . thereafter hun9 hr the neclc.'

Upon its own scrutiny of the evidence, the Court was 'fully satisfied that the conclusion recorded by the learned Sessions Judge and by the High Court, that the appellants are guilty of the. murder of the deceased in a most brutai and heinous fashion, is perfectly . correct and sound.'
why_respondent_won: The findings of the lower courts, which convicted the appellants, were affirmed as 'perfectly correct and sound.'

The circumstantial evidence, supported by medical evidence, was deemed sufficient to lead to the 'only conclusion that the deceased was murdered in a most brutal and heinpus fashion and then hung by rope by the accused so as to give an appearance of a case of suicide.'
policy_considerations: The Court observed that 'instances of bride killing are. alarmingly on the increase' and described it as an 'unfortunate and disturbing phenomenon' and a 'growing evil.'

The Court stated that 'it is imperative that whenever dastardly crimes of this nature are detected and the offence brought home to the accused, the courts must deal with the offender most ruthlessly and impose deterrent punishment.'
